questions.title: The four methods
questions.text: Select the **four** methods of system implementation (changeover).

options.content: Direct
Parallel
Prototyping
Pilot
Phased
Black-box testing

scheme.mark_scheme: A and B and D and E. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: The four changeover methods are direct, parallel, pilot and phased. Prototyping is a design technique; black-box testing is a testing method.

questions.title: The implementation stage
questions.text: Which statement best describes the **implementation** stage of the system life cycle?

options.content: Finding out what the users need by interviews and questionnaires
Installing the new system, converting the data, training the users and changing over from the old system
Drawing DFDs and designing the database
Fixing faults and adding features after the system has been used for a year

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Implementation = install, convert data, train, change over. A is analysis, C is design, D is maintenance.

questions.title: Match the descriptions
questions.text: Match each implementation method to its description.

right.text: The old system stops and the new one starts on the same day
Old and new systems run together and results are compared
The whole new system is first used in one department
The new system is introduced one part at a time

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R1, L2–R2, L3–R3, L4–R4. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Tasks in every implementation
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

Whatever method is used, the existing records must be moved into the new system — this is called data [[1]]. Users must also be [[2]] to use the new system. With [[3]] changeover the old system is stopped and the new one starts on the same day.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) conversion (2) trained (3) direct
scheme.explanation: Data conversion and training are needed with every method; direct changeover switches over in one day.

questions.title: The safest method
questions.text: Direct changeover is the safest method because the new system is used by everyone immediately.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Direct changeover is the riskiest; parallel running is the safest because the old system remains as a backup.

questions.title: What pilot means
questions.text: In pilot implementation, every department receives one module of the new system at a time.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: That describes **phased** implementation. In a pilot, the **whole** system is used in **one** department or branch first.

questions.title: Direct changeover
questions.text: Tick (✓) to show whether each statement is an advantage or a disadvantage of **direct** changeover.

prefill: It is the fastest way to start using the new system
There is no backup system if the new system fails
Only one system has to be run, so it is cheap
All staff must be trained before the changeover date

scheme.mark_scheme: It is the fastest way to start using the new system — Advantage (1); There is no backup system if the new system fails — Disadvantage (1); Only one system has to be run, so it is cheap — Advantage (1); All staff must be trained before the changeover date — Disadvantage (1)
scheme.model_answer: It is the fastest way to start using the new system — Advantage; There is no backup system if the new system fails — Disadvantage; Only one system has to be run, so it is cheap — Advantage; All staff must be trained before the changeover date — Disadvantage.
scheme.explanation: Direct is fast and cheap, but there is no fallback and everyone must be ready on day one.

questions.title: Parallel running
questions.text: Tick (✓) to show whether each statement is an advantage or a disadvantage of **parallel** running.

prefill: Staff have to enter the same data twice
Results of the new system can be compared with the old one
It is the most expensive method
The old system is still available if the new one fails

scheme.mark_scheme: Staff have to enter the same data twice — Disadvantage (1); Results of the new system can be compared with the old one — Advantage (1); It is the most expensive method — Disadvantage (1); The old system is still available if the new one fails — Advantage (1)
scheme.model_answer: Staff have to enter the same data twice — Disadvantage; Results of the new system can be compared with the old one — Advantage; It is the most expensive method — Disadvantage; The old system is still available if the new one fails — Advantage.
scheme.explanation: Parallel is safe because the old system is a backup and results can be compared, but it doubles the work and cost.

questions.title: Which method
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the method described.

prefill: The safest method, but the most expensive
The fastest and cheapest, but the most risky
One branch of a bank uses the new system before the others
The accounts module is introduced first, then stock control, then payroll

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Parallel (1); 2 Direct (1); 3 Pilot (1); 4 Phased (1)

questions.title: Pilot or phased
questions.text: Which statement correctly compares **pilot** and **phased** implementation?

options.content: Pilot introduces one module everywhere; phased introduces the whole system in one branch
Pilot introduces the whole system in one part of the organisation first, whereas phased introduces one module at a time across the whole organisation
Both stop the old system everywhere on the same day
Pilot keeps both systems running everywhere and compares the results

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Pilot = whole system, one place. Phased = one part, everywhere. Option D describes parallel running.

questions.title: Most expensive
questions.text: State the implementation method that is usually the **most expensive** because two systems are run at the same time.

scheme.mark_scheme: parallel
scheme.explanation: Parallel running doubles the work: both systems are run and the data is entered into both.

questions.title: A backup during changeover
questions.text: Select the **two** methods in which an old system (or old parts of it) is still in use somewhere in the organisation while the new system is introduced, so problems do not stop the whole organisation.

options.content: Direct
Parallel
Pilot
Big bang

scheme.mark_scheme: B and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Parallel keeps the old system everywhere; pilot keeps it at the other sites. Direct (big bang) switches it off everywhere at once.

questions.title: A seaport system
questions.text: Suggest an implementation method: *A system that tracks the arrival of cargo ships at the seaport is being replaced.*

scheme.mark_scheme: Parallel (1)
scheme.model_answer: Parallel

questions.title: A café
questions.text: Suggest an implementation method: *A café is introducing a system that allows customers to complete their orders electronically instead of ordering from the staff. The management wants the change to happen quickly and cheaply.*

scheme.mark_scheme: Direct (1)
scheme.model_answer: Direct

questions.title: A school's clubs
questions.text: Suggest an implementation method: *A school introduces a new system for managing hobby clubs. The old system is a paper log. The new system is first used by one grade, and later by the whole school.*

scheme.mark_scheme: Pilot (1)
scheme.model_answer: Pilot

questions.title: Phased implementation
questions.text: For which system is **phased** implementation most suitable?

options.content: A small shop's single till program
A hospital system with separate modules for patients, prescriptions and billing
A new organisation with no old system
A system that must be compared with the old one for a month

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: Phased implementation suits large systems that can be divided into independent modules.

questions.title: A clinic changes over
questions.text: A clinic is replacing its paper patient records with a computer system. Patient safety depends on the records being correct. Which choice and reason are best?

options.content: Direct — it is the cheapest, so the clinic saves money
Parallel — the paper records stay in use as a backup and the new records can be checked against them
Phased — because the clinic has only one building
Pilot — because every clinic must use a pilot

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Patient records are critical, so the old records are kept as a backup and results are compared — parallel running. The justification must link to the scenario.

questions.title: A supermarket chain
questions.text: A supermarket chain with **40 shops** across Kazakhstan is replacing its stock-control system. All shops sell the same products and use the same procedures. Which method is most suitable?

options.content: Direct in all 40 shops on the same day
Pilot — introduce it in one shop first, fix problems, then roll it out to the other 39
Parallel in all 40 shops for a year
Phased — because the shops are similar

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Many similar sites → pilot. Problems found in one shop are fixed before they can affect all 40 shops; parallel in every shop would be very expensive.

questions.title: A national bank
questions.text: A national bank is replacing the software that processes all customer payments, and recommends **parallel running**. Select the **two** statements that justify this choice.

options.content: Payments are critical, so a failure with no backup would be unacceptable
It is the cheapest method
The results of the new software can be checked against the old software before the old one is switched off
Staff will have less work during the changeover
It is the fastest method

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Parallel is chosen for safety and checking. It is the most expensive and slowest method and doubles staff work.

questions.title: Data conversion
questions.text: Which statement best describes **data conversion** during implementation?

options.content: Training users to enter data in the new system
Transferring the existing data from the old system into the format of the new system and then checking it
Choosing the date when the old system will be switched off
Writing the user guide for the new system

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Data conversion moves existing records (paper cards or old files) into the new system's format — and checks them.

questions.title: Checking typed records
questions.text: A clinic types its paper patient cards into the new database. A second person then compares each typed record with the paper card. State the name of this check.

scheme.mark_scheme: verification
scheme.explanation: Comparing the typed record with the source document is verification; it finds typing errors that validation cannot.

questions.title: Why implementation is risky
questions.text: Implementation is often the most risky stage because, for the first time, the new system meets real data, real users and real workload.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.
scheme.explanation: Testing used test data and a small group of testers; implementation is the first time the system has to work for real while the organisation cannot stop working.

questions.title: Training and the method
questions.text: Match each implementation method to how staff training usually fits it.

right.text: Every user must be trained before the changeover day
Staff can be trained gradually while the old system still works
Staff at one site are trained first and later help to train the others
Staff learn the system one module at a time

scheme.mark_scheme: Direct – Every user must be trained before the changeover day; Parallel – Staff can be trained gradually while the old system still works; Pilot – Staff at one site are trained first and later help to train the others; Phased – Staff learn the system one module at a time. One mark per correct match.
scheme.explanation: Training must fit the method: all at once for direct, gradually for parallel, one site first for pilot, one module at a time for phased.

questions.title: Recognise the method
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the method that fits the statement best.

prefill: The full system is in use only after all the parts have been introduced
The natural choice for an organisation with many similar branches
Staff workload doubles because every transaction is processed twice
Suitable when the old system no longer works at all

scheme.mark_scheme: The full system is in use only after all the parts have been introduced — Phased (1); The natural choice for an organisation with many similar branches — Pilot (1); Staff workload doubles because every transaction is processed twice — Parallel (1); Suitable when the old system no longer works at all — Direct (1)
scheme.model_answer: The full system is in use only after all the parts have been introduced — Phased; The natural choice for an organisation with many similar branches — Pilot; Staff workload doubles because every transaction is processed twice — Parallel; Suitable when the old system no longer works at all — Direct.
scheme.explanation: Phased is the slowest; pilot suits many similar sites; parallel doubles the work; direct is used when there is nothing to run alongside.

questions.title: Factors in the choice
questions.text: Select the **three** factors that analysts consider when choosing an implementation method.

options.content: How critical the system is — what happens if it fails for a day
Whether the organisation has several similar sites or the system has separate modules
The budget and staff available for extra work
The colour scheme of the new interface
The number of letters in the system's name

scheme.mark_scheme: A and B and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Criticality, organisation structure, budget and staff (and also time, similarity of the systems and how well it was tested) decide the choice.

questions.title: When parallel running makes little sense
questions.text: A city council replaces paper application forms handled by staff with **online self-service** that works in a completely different way. Why may parallel running be unsuitable here?

options.content: Parallel running is always the cheapest, so it would waste no money
The two systems cannot easily process the same data and produce comparable results, so there is little to compare
Parallel running needs several similar branches
Parallel running cannot keep the old system as a backup

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Parallel running depends on entering the same data into both systems and comparing the outputs; if the systems work in completely different ways the comparison is not possible.

questions.title: A fixed deadline
questions.text: A small shop's old till software **stops working when its licence expires in one week**. The new system is simple and well tested. Which method is most suitable?

options.content: Parallel running for three months
Phased, one module per month
Direct changeover on the day the licence expires
Pilot in one of its branches

scheme.mark_scheme: C.
scheme.explanation: The old system will be unusable after the deadline, the shop is small and the system is simple, so a quick, cheap direct changeover fits.

questions.title: Combining methods
questions.text: Methods can be combined — for example, a bank may run a pilot in one branch and use parallel running inside that branch for the first month.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.
scheme.explanation: Combinations are common: a pilot site may itself change over in parallel, and each phase of a phased rollout may be piloted in one department first.

questions.title: A new library system for Qalam Libraries
questions.text: **Qalam Libraries** runs 15 public libraries in one region. All branches use the same procedures. The old loans software is being replaced by a new web-based system with three modules: catalogue, loans and fines.

parts.title: Methods
parts.text: List the **four** methods of system implementation.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- any two of direct, parallel, pilot, phased (1)
- all four (2)
scheme.model_answer: Direct, parallel, pilot, phased.

parts.title: Which method
parts.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the implementation method described.

prefill: The whole new system is used in one branch first
The old system stops on Friday and the new one starts on Monday
Both systems are used and their results compared for two months
The catalogue module is introduced first, then loans, then fines

scheme.mark_scheme: The whole new system is used in one branch first — Pilot (1); The old system stops on Friday and the new one starts on Monday — Direct (1); Both systems are used and their results compared for two months — Parallel (1); The catalogue module is introduced first, then loans, then fines — Phased (1)
scheme.model_answer: The whole new system is used in one branch first — Pilot; The old system stops on Friday and the new one starts on Monday — Direct; Both systems are used and their results compared for two months — Parallel; The catalogue module is introduced first, then loans, then fines — Phased.

parts.title: Pilot for the libraries
parts.text: The manager chooses **pilot** implementation. Explain why this method is suitable for Qalam Libraries.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- there are 15 similar branches with the same procedures, so one branch can try the whole system first (1)
- problems are found and fixed there before the other 14 branches change over / only one branch is affected if it fails (1)

points.criterion: Problems fixed before rollout / limited effect

scheme.model_answer: All 15 branches work in the same way, so one branch can use the whole system first; any faults are fixed there, and only that branch is affected, before the other 14 change over.

parts.title: Disadvantage of pilot
parts.text: Describe **one** disadvantage of pilot implementation for Qalam Libraries.

scheme.mark_scheme:
One disadvantage, identified (1) and described in context (1), e.g.:
- takes longer before all branches use the system (1) — the other 14 branches keep the old software for months (1)
- the pilot branch may not be typical (1) — problems that only appear in larger branches are missed (1)
- two systems in use at once (1) — books borrowed in one branch and returned to another may be recorded in different systems (1)
- if the pilot fails, that branch is still badly affected (1) — its readers cannot borrow books (1)
scheme.model_answer: During the pilot two different systems are in use: a reader who borrows a book in the pilot branch and returns it to another branch may not have the loan recorded correctly.

questions.title: Patient records at a regional hospital
questions.text: A regional hospital in Kostanay is replacing its old patient-record and prescription software. Doctors use the records 24 hours a day, and wrong or missing information could put patients at risk.

parts.title: Choose a method
parts.text: Identify the most suitable implementation method for the hospital and justify your choice.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- parallel running (1)
- the system is critical / errors could harm patients (1)
- the old system remains as a backup and the new system's results can be compared / checked before the old one is stopped (1)
scheme.model_answer: Parallel running. Patient safety depends on the records, so the old software keeps running as a backup and every result of the new system can be checked against it before the old one is switched off.

parts.title: Disadvantages
parts.text: Explain **two** disadvantages of the method you chose in (a) for the hospital.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two disadvantages, each identified (1) and explained in context (1), e.g. (for parallel):
- most expensive (1) — two systems must be run / maintained, extra staff costs (1)
- double workload (1) — nurses / doctors enter every record twice, less time for patients / more errors (1)
- takes longer to complete (1) — benefits of the new system arrive later (1)
- staff may keep relying on the old system (1)
Accept disadvantages of another method if (a) chose it.
scheme.model_answer: It is expensive, because the hospital pays to run and support both systems for weeks. It also doubles the workload: nurses must enter every prescription into both systems, which takes time away from patients and makes typing errors more likely.

parts.title: Why not direct
parts.text: Explain why **direct** changeover would **not** be suitable for the hospital.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- with direct changeover the old system is stopped completely on one day (1)
- if the new system fails there is no backup / records may be lost or unavailable (1)
- doctors could not see patient records / prescriptions, putting patients at risk (1)
scheme.model_answer: Direct changeover switches the old software off on one day. If the new system then fails, there is nothing to fall back on, so doctors could not see records or prescriptions and patients could be harmed.

questions.title: Electronic ordering at the Dastarkhan café
questions.text: The **Dastarkhan** café has one small restaurant. Customers will now order on a tablet at their table instead of ordering from a waiter. The owner wants the change to happen **quickly and cheaply**.

parts.title: Direct changeover
parts.text: Describe **direct** changeover.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the old system / method is stopped completely (1)
- and the new system starts immediately / on the same day, with no overlap (1)
scheme.model_answer: The old way of ordering is stopped completely and the new tablet system is used from the very next day, with no overlap.

parts.title: Advantages for the café
parts.text: Explain **two** advantages of direct changeover for the café.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two advantages, each identified (1) and explained in context (1), e.g.:
- cheapest (1) — only one system is run, no double work / no extra staff, matches the owner's wish (1)
- fastest (1) — customers use tablets immediately, benefits at once (1)
- staff do not use two systems (1) — less confusion for waiters (1)
- simple to plan (1) — small café, one site (1)
scheme.model_answer: It is the cheapest method because the café runs only one system and waiters do not have to take orders twice. It is also the fastest, so customers can order on the tablets straight away, which is what the owner wants.

parts.title: Reducing the risk
parts.text: Suggest **two** things the owner could do to reduce the risk of direct changeover.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): test the new system thoroughly before the changeover date; train all staff before the changeover; change over on a quiet day / when the café is closed; keep paper order pads ready as an emergency fallback; back up the menu / data; have technical support available on the first day
scheme.model_answer: Test the tablet system fully and train every waiter before the changeover day, and keep paper order pads ready in case the tablets fail.

parts.title: Direct and parallel
parts.text: Compare direct changeover and parallel running in terms of **cost** and **risk**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- cost: direct is cheaper / cheapest, whereas parallel is the most expensive (two systems, double work) (1)
- risk: direct is the most risky (no backup), whereas parallel is the safest (old system as backup) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Direct changeover is the cheapest method, whereas parallel running is the most expensive because two systems run together. Direct is also the most risky because there is no backup, whereas parallel is the safest because the old system is still available.

questions.title: A management system for Zhuldyz College
questions.text: **Zhuldyz College** is introducing a new management system with three separate modules: **attendance**, **marks** and **reports to parents**. The college has one campus and 900 students.

parts.title: Phased implementation
parts.text: Describe **phased** implementation.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the new system is introduced one module / part at a time (1)
- across the whole organisation; the next part is introduced when the previous one works (1)

points.criterion: Whole organisation / next when previous works

scheme.model_answer: The new system is introduced one module at a time for the whole college — for example attendance first, and marks only when attendance is working.

parts.title: Phased and parallel
parts.text: Compare **phased** implementation and **parallel** running for the college. Refer to cost, risk and time.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Up to 4 marks; comparative points (whereas / but) about both methods:
- phased introduces one module at a time, whereas parallel runs the whole old and new systems together (1)
- parallel is more expensive / double workload for teachers, phased spreads the cost (1)
- parallel is safer – full backup; phased: only the current module is at risk (1)
- phased is slowest – full system only after all phases; parallel ends once results match (1)
- phased lets staff learn gradually; parallel lets results be compared directly (1)
Max 2 if only one method is described.
scheme.model_answer: Phased introduces attendance, then marks, then reports, whereas parallel runs the whole old and new systems side by side. Parallel is more expensive because teachers enter every mark twice, while phased spreads the cost. Parallel is safer because the old system is a complete backup, whereas phased risks only the module being introduced. Phased is the slowest, because reports to parents arrive only after the other phases.

parts.title: Recommend
parts.text: Recommend an implementation method for Zhuldyz College. Justify your recommendation and explain why **one** other method is less suitable.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- recommended method (phased most likely; accept any method with a valid scenario-based justification) (1)
- justification linked to the scenario, e.g. three separate modules / staff learn one at a time / errors in one module fixed before the next (1)
- a second justification point or the trade-off accepted (cost / time) (1)
- one other method rejected with a scenario-linked reason, e.g. pilot unsuitable because there is only one campus; direct too risky for 900 students' marks; parallel too much double work for teachers (1)
scheme.model_answer: Phased implementation. The system already has three separate modules, so attendance can be introduced first and its problems fixed before marks and reports are added, and teachers learn one part at a time. It takes longer, but the risk to 900 students' marks is small. Pilot is less suitable because the college has only one campus, so there is no similar site to try it on first.

questions.title: A new stock system for the Shipa pharmacy chain
questions.text: The **Shipa** pharmacy chain has **25 pharmacies** in Almaty and Konaev. All pharmacies sell the same medicines and follow the same procedures. The chain is replacing its old stock and sales software with a new system. The old software holds about **12 000 product records**, which must be moved into the new database.

parts.title: Tasks of implementation
parts.text: Apart from changing over from the old system, state **two** tasks that must be carried out during the implementation of the new system.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any two (1 each):
- install the hardware / network / software
- convert / transfer the existing data (product records) into the new database
- train the staff / users
- hand over the user guide / technical documentation
Do not accept: analysis, design, testing the program code, changeover itself.
scheme.model_answer: Converting the 12 000 product records from the old software into the new database, and training the pharmacists to use the new system.

parts.title: Name the method
parts.text: Draw a line to link each plan the managers discussed to the implementation method it describes.

left.text: Close every pharmacy's old software on 31 December and use only the new system from 1 January
Use the new system in the Konaev pharmacy for six weeks, then in all the others
Record every sale in both the old and the new software for one month and compare the stock levels
Start with the stock module in all pharmacies; add the sales module two months later

scheme.mark_scheme: Close every pharmacy's old software on 31 December and use only the new system from 1 January – direct; use the new system in the Konaev pharmacy for six weeks, then in all the others – pilot; record every sale in both the old and the new software for one month and compare the stock levels – parallel; start with the stock module in all pharmacies, add the sales module two months later – phased (1 each)
scheme.model_answer: 31 December / 1 January → direct; Konaev pharmacy first → pilot; every sale in both systems and compare → parallel; stock module first, sales module later → phased.

parts.title: Checking the converted data
parts.text: The product records are exported from the old software and imported into the new database. Explain how the chain can check that **no records were lost or changed** during this data conversion.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- compare record counts / totals in both systems, e.g. number of products and total stock value (1)
- if the counts / totals match, no records were lost; any difference is investigated before changeover (1)
OR
- verification: a sample of records is compared with the old system / double entry compared by the computer (1) … so changed or wrongly copied values are found (1)

points.criterion: How it shows records are complete / correct

scheme.model_answer: After importing, they count the product records and add up the total stock quantity in both the old and the new system. If both show 12 000 products and the same totals, nothing was lost; they also compare a sample of records field by field to find any values that were changed during conversion.

questions.title: An ambulance dispatch system in Karaganda
questions.text: The emergency dispatch centre in **Karaganda** receives all 103 calls for the city. Operators record each call, the address and the type of emergency, and the system chooses the nearest free ambulance. The centre works **24 hours a day**. It is replacing its old dispatch software with a new system that also shows the position of every ambulance on a map.

parts.title: Choose a method
parts.text: Identify the most suitable implementation method for the dispatch centre and justify your choice.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- parallel running (1)
- the system is critical: a failure could delay ambulances / put lives at risk / the centre works 24 hours so it cannot stop (1)
- the old system stays as a backup if the new one fails / the results (chosen ambulance) of both systems can be compared before the old one is switched off (1)
Accept pilot only with a clear scenario reason (e.g. one district / shift first) for max 2.

points.criterion: Further reason / how it reduces the risk

scheme.model_answer: Parallel running. A fault in dispatch software could delay an ambulance and cost lives, and the centre cannot stop working at any time. With parallel running the old software keeps working as a backup, and the ambulance chosen by the new system can be compared with the old one until the new system is shown to be reliable.

parts.title: How it works here
parts.text: Describe how parallel running would be carried out at the dispatch centre.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- every call is recorded in both the old and the new software at the same time / both systems run together (1)
- the outputs (ambulance chosen, times) are compared and the old system is switched off only when the new one has given correct results for the planned period (1)

points.criterion: Both systems / every call entered twice
Compare results, then switch off old

scheme.model_answer: For a planned period every call is entered into both the old and the new software. The ambulance chosen and the records produced by each are compared; differences are investigated and fixed. When the new system has worked correctly for the whole period, the old software is switched off.

parts.title: Length of the period
parts.text: The manager wants parallel running to last for **one week only**. Explain why a longer period, such as a full month, would be better.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- one week may not include every kind of processing / situation, e.g. busy holiday nights, rare emergency types, month-end reports (1)
- faults that appear only in those situations would not be found before the old system (the backup) is switched off (1)

points.criterion: Faults found before old system removed

scheme.model_answer: In one week the new system may not meet every situation — a holiday night with many calls, a rare type of emergency or the monthly report. Running in parallel for a full month means more of these cases are tested while the old system is still there as a backup, so faults are found before it is removed.

parts.title: Double workload
parts.text: During parallel running the operators must enter every call twice. Explain **one** problem this could cause for the dispatch centre.

scheme.mark_scheme:
One problem explained (2): e.g.
- operators are overworked / tired (1) so they make more data-entry mistakes / respond more slowly to calls (1)
- the centre needs extra staff / overtime (1) so the changeover is expensive (1)
- entering twice takes longer (1) so callers wait longer for help (1)
- mistakes in one copy (1) make the comparison of results unreliable / hard (1)
scheme.model_answer: Entering every call twice takes each operator longer, so callers may wait longer before an ambulance is sent; tired operators also make more typing mistakes, which makes the comparison of the two systems less reliable.

questions.title: Contactless fares on the Aktobe city buses
questions.text: The bus company of **Aktobe** runs **300 buses on 20 routes**. It is introducing a new fare system: passengers pay by tapping a bank card or phone on a reader instead of paying the driver in cash. Every bus will have the same reader. The company plans to use **pilot implementation**.

parts.title: Pilot implementation
parts.text: Describe **pilot** implementation, using the bus company as an example.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the whole new system is introduced in one part of the organisation first, e.g. the buses of one route (1)
- when it works well there, it is introduced on all the other routes (1)

points.criterion: Whole system in one part first
Then rolled out to the rest

scheme.model_answer: The complete new fare system is first installed on the buses of one route only while the other 19 routes keep taking cash. When it has worked well there, it is rolled out to all the other routes.

parts.title: Advantages of the pilot
parts.text: Explain **two** advantages of pilot implementation for the bus company.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two advantages, each explained (2 + 2), e.g.
- if the readers / software fail, only one route is affected (1) the other 19 routes keep working / passengers can still travel and pay (1)
- faults are found in real use and fixed before the full rollout (1) so all 300 buses get a tested system (1)
- the drivers on the pilot route become experienced (1) and can train / support the other drivers (1)
- cheaper / less work than parallel running on every bus (1) because cash and card do not have to be compared on all routes (1)
scheme.model_answer: First, if the readers or the payment software fail, only the buses of one route are affected; the other 19 routes carry on as normal. Second, the problems found on the pilot route — for example readers that are slow when the bus is full — can be fixed before the system goes on all 300 buses, and the pilot drivers can then help to train the others.

parts.title: Choosing the pilot route
parts.text: The company chooses a quiet suburban route with few passengers for the pilot. Explain why this choice could be a problem.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the quiet route is not typical of the other / busy city-centre routes (1)
- problems that happen only with many passengers (queues at the reader, slow network, many taps per minute) will not be found until the full rollout, when all buses are affected (1)

points.criterion: Problems found only later on busy routes

scheme.model_answer: A quiet route is not typical of the busy city-centre routes. Problems that appear only when many passengers tap at once — queues, slow reader responses, network overload — will not show up in the pilot and will only be discovered after the system is on all routes.

questions.title: A management system for the Altyn Tau hotel
questions.text: The **Altyn Tau** hotel in Shymkent has 180 rooms. Its new management system has three modules: **bookings**, **restaurant billing** and **housekeeping**. A guest's restaurant bill is added to the room bill in the bookings module. The manager is deciding between pilot and phased implementation.

parts.title: Pilot or phased
parts.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show whether the statement describes **pilot** or **phased** implementation.

prefill: The whole new system is first used in one part of the organisation
Old and new parts of the system must exchange data during the changeover
Most suitable for an organisation with many similar branches
Everyone in the organisation starts using the same new module at the same time

scheme.mark_scheme: Row 1 Pilot (1); Row 2 Phased (1); Row 3 Pilot (1); Row 4 Phased (1)
scheme.model_answer: Whole system in one part first — Pilot; old and new parts exchange data — Phased; many similar branches — Pilot; everyone uses the same new module at once — Phased.

parts.title: A difficulty of phased
parts.text: The hotel introduces the bookings module first. Explain **one** difficulty this causes while restaurant billing is still done with the old system.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the old restaurant billing system and the new bookings module must exchange data / a temporary link (interface) must be built (1)
- otherwise restaurant bills may not be added to the room bill / must be copied by hand, causing errors or guests being charged wrongly (1)

points.criterion: Old and new parts must work together

scheme.model_answer: The guest's restaurant bill is still produced by the old system but must be added to the room bill in the new bookings module. A temporary link has to be built or staff must copy the bills by hand, which is extra work and can lead to guests being charged wrongly when they check out.

parts.title: Why not pilot
parts.text: State **one** reason why pilot implementation is **not** suitable for the Altyn Tau hotel.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any one (1):
- the hotel has only one site / no similar branches to try the whole system on first
- the departments share the same guest bills, so one part of the hotel cannot use a different system from the rest
scheme.model_answer: The hotel is a single site with no similar branches, so there is nowhere to try the whole system first.

questions.title: A new billing system for Shygys Energy
questions.text: **Shygys Energy** supplies electricity to **400 000 homes** in East Kazakhstan. It has **6 customer offices**. Its billing system has three modules: **meter readings**, **bills** and **payments**. Customers who are not billed correctly may have their electricity cut off by mistake. The licence for the old software **expires in four months**, and the company has a limited budget.

parts.title: Evaluate and recommend
parts.text: Evaluate the **four** implementation methods for Shygys Energy and recommend the most suitable one.

scheme.mark_scheme:
One mark per method evaluated with a point linked to the scenario (max 4):
- direct: fastest / cheapest and fits the four-month deadline and limited budget, but no backup — wrong bills for 400 000 homes / electricity cut off by mistake (1)
- parallel: safest, old system is a backup and bills can be compared, but most expensive / double work for a limited budget and may not finish before the licence expires (1)
- pilot: one office first limits the risk to its customers and its staff can train the others, but the rollout to 6 offices takes longer / the data of all offices is in one billing system (1)
- phased: modules one at a time (meter readings first), errors limited to one function, but the slowest method and old and new modules must exchange data (readings → bills) (1)
Recommendation (2):
- a justified recommendation linked to the scenario, e.g. pilot in one office, or a combined plan such as pilot with a short parallel period at the pilot office (1)
- states the trade-off accepted, e.g. more time / cost than direct but risk limited to a small group of customers within the deadline (1)
Any method may be recommended if justified; a recommendation of phased or parallel must address the deadline.

points.criterion: Trade-off of the recommended method acknowledged

scheme.model_answer: Direct changeover is the fastest and cheapest, which suits the deadline and budget, but if the new bills are wrong there is no backup and up to 400 000 homes could be overcharged or cut off. Parallel running is the safest because every bill can be compared with the old system, but processing everything twice is expensive and slow for a company with a limited budget, and it may not finish before the licence expires. Phased implementation would introduce meter readings, then bills, then payments, so a fault affects only one function, but it is the slowest method and the old bills module would need data from the new readings module. Pilot implementation would start with the customers of one office, so a fault affects only a small group and that office's staff can train the others; it takes longer than direct but can be completed within four months. I recommend a pilot in one office, with that office's bills checked against the old system for the first month. It costs more than direct changeover, but it keeps the risk to a small group of customers and stays within the deadline and budget.

parts.title: The cheapest method
parts.text: Explain why **direct** changeover is the cheapest implementation method.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- only one system is run / maintained after the changeover date; no old hardware or software to keep (1)
- staff do no double data entry / no overtime, and the changeover takes the shortest time (1)
scheme.model_answer: After the changeover date only the new system is used, so the company does not pay to keep the old software and hardware running, and staff never enter data twice or work overtime; the whole changeover is also over in a day.

summary: The four methods of implementing (changing over to) a new system — direct, parallel, pilot and phased — how each works, their advantages and disadvantages compared on speed, cost and risk, and how to choose and justify the right method for a scenario.

blocks.content: The stage of the system life cycle in which the **new system is installed and put into use**, replacing the **old system**. It includes installing hardware and software, **transferring (converting) data** from the old system, **training** staff and **changing over** to the new way of working.

The **plan for how the old system is replaced by the new one** — all at once, side by side, in one place first, or one part at a time. The four methods are **direct**, **parallel**, **pilot** and **phased**.

items.title: Tasks in every implementation
items.content:
- **Install** the hardware, network and software.
- **Convert data** — move the existing records into the new system's files or database, and check them.
- **Train** the users and the technical staff.
- Hand over the **user guide** and **technical documentation**.
- **Change over** from the old system using the chosen method.

items.title: Why the method matters
items.content:
- If the new system has a fault, the organisation may **lose data** or be **unable to work**.
- Some methods keep the **old system as a backup**; others do not.
- The methods differ in **speed**, **cost**, **risk** and **staff workload**.
- The right choice depends on **how critical** the system is and how the organisation is **organised**.

blocks.content: Transferring the existing data from the old system (paper files or old software) into the **format of the new system**, then **checking** it — e.g. typing paper patient cards into the new database, or exporting old records and importing them.

blocks.text: Why implementation is a risky moment

blocks.content: By the time a system reaches implementation it has been analysed, designed, developed and tested. Yet implementation is often the **most dangerous** stage of the whole life cycle, because for the first time the system meets **real data, real users and real workload**. Testing uses test data and a small number of testers; on the first working day a clinic's system must handle hundreds of real patients, receptionists who are still learning, and records copied from an old system that may contain errors. Faults that testing missed appear exactly when the organisation depends on the system.

At the same time the organisation **cannot stop working** while it changes systems. A shop must keep selling, a hospital must keep treating patients, a school must keep recording attendance. The implementation method is the organisation's answer to the question: *how do we move from the old way of working to the new one without losing data or stopping our work if something goes wrong?*

blocks.text: Data conversion and training in more detail

blocks.content: **Data conversion** is often the biggest single job of implementation. If the old system is on **paper**, every record must be typed in — usually by staff or temporary data-entry workers — and then checked by **verification** (a second person compares the typed record with the paper card, or the data is entered twice and the computer compares both copies). If the old system is **electronic**, the data is **exported** from it, **transformed** into the new structure (for example one "name" field split into surname and first name, dates changed from MM/DD to DD.MM) and **imported** into the new database. After conversion, record counts and totals are compared (e.g. "1 250 patients and 18 340 visits in both systems") to make sure nothing was lost.

Conversion takes time, and during that time the old system keeps changing — new patients arrive, new sales are made. This is one reason the choice of method matters: with **direct** changeover the conversion must be finished and checked **before** the changeover date; with **parallel** running new data is entered into both systems anyway; with **pilot** and **phased** methods only part of the data needs converting at each step.

**Training** must also fit the method. With direct changeover every user must be trained before the same day; with pilot implementation only the pilot site's staff are trained first, and they later help to train others; with phased implementation staff learn one module at a time. Without training even a perfect system fails, because users make mistakes, work slowly and lose trust in it.
There are **four** implementation methods. They differ in **how quickly** the old system is replaced and **how much risk** the organisation takes if the new system fails.

blocks.caption: The four implementation methods over time (dark bar = old system, light bar = new system)

blocks.content:
- Writing "testing" or "analysis" as an implementation method — the four methods are **direct, parallel, pilot, phased**.
- Forgetting that **data conversion and training** are needed whichever method is chosen.
The old system is **stopped completely** and the new system is **started immediately** in its place, on a fixed date ("big bang").

With direct changeover the organisation chooses a **changeover date** — often a weekend or a holiday, when the workload is low. Before that date all data is converted and checked, all staff are trained and the new hardware and software are installed and tested. On the changeover day the old system is **switched off** and from that moment all work is done with the new system only. There is no going back: the old system is not updated any more, so even if it is still physically there, its data is soon out of date.

The method is attractive because it is **simple, fast and cheap**: there is only one system to run, staff do not do any work twice, and the benefits of the new system start immediately. Its weakness is that it puts **all the risk on one day**. If the new system has a serious fault, the whole organisation is affected at once and has **no working system to fall back on**. For that reason direct changeover is chosen when a failure would be an inconvenience rather than a disaster, when the new system has been very thoroughly tested, or when there is no alternative — for example when the old system has broken down or the new system is so different that both cannot be run together.

blocks.title: Direct changeover
rows: **Fastest** method — the benefits of the new system arrive immediately
**Most risky** — if the new system fails there is **no backup** system to fall back on
**Cheapest** — only one system is run, no duplicate work
Data may be **lost** or the organisation may **stop working** if there are errors
Staff never have to use two systems at once
**All staff** must be trained **before** the changeover date
Problems affect the **whole organisation** at once

blocks.title: When direct changeover is suitable
blocks.content:
- A **café** introduces electronic ordering instead of ordering from staff — small, simple system; a short failure is not dangerous.
- The old system **no longer works**, or is so different that running both is impossible.
- A **new organisation** with no old system at all.

The **old and new systems run at the same time** for a period. The same data is entered into **both** and the **results are compared**. When the new system has been shown to be reliable, the old one is stopped.

During parallel running every transaction is processed **twice**: once in the old system and once in the new. A payroll clerk, for example, calculates the salaries for March in the old program and also in the new one, and then the **outputs are compared** line by line. If they agree, the new system is trusted a little more; if they differ, the cause is found and fixed — while the employees are still paid correctly from the old system. The period of parallel running is planned in advance (for example **one full month**, or one complete cycle such as a term or a quarter, so that every kind of processing is checked at least once). When the new system has produced correct results for the whole period, management decides to **switch off the old system**.

The great strength of parallel running is that the old system acts as a **live backup**: if the new system fails, work simply continues on the old one, and no data is lost. Its price is **cost and effort**: staff must enter all data twice, often working overtime or with temporary help; two sets of hardware and software must be kept running; and the comparison of results takes time. Tired staff entering everything twice also make more mistakes, which can make the comparison harder. Parallel running is therefore chosen when a failure would be **very expensive or dangerous** and the organisation can afford the extra cost.

blocks.title: Parallel running
rows: **Safest** — the old system is a **backup** if the new one fails
**Most expensive** — two systems, extra staff time
The new system's results can be **checked against** the old one
**Double workload** — data entered twice; staff may be overworked and make errors
Staff can be **trained gradually** while the old system still works
No data is lost if the new system fails
Staff may keep relying on the old system

blocks.title: When parallel running is suitable
blocks.content:
- **Critical** systems where failure is unacceptable: a **seaport** tracking cargo ships, **hospital** records, **banking**, **payroll**, air-traffic data.
- When the new system's results **must be checked** against the old one (e.g. the first month of a new payroll).

blocks.title: Direct and parallel — the two extremes
rows: Old system after the changeover date
Backup if the new system fails

blocks.content:
- Saying parallel running is "fast" or "cheap" — it is the **most expensive** method and slow, but the **safest**.
- Writing only "it is risky" for direct — say **why**: there is **no old system to fall back on** if the new one fails.
The **whole new system** is introduced in **one part of the organisation first** — one department, branch, shop or class. When it works well there, it is introduced in all the other parts.
The new system is introduced **gradually, one part (module / function) at a time**, across the **whole organisation**. Each phase is introduced only when the previous one works.

blocks.caption: Pilot = the whole system in one place first; phased = one part of the system everywhere at a time

blocks.content: Pilot implementation uses one part of the organisation as a **real-life test site**. A supermarket chain with 40 shops installs the new checkout system in **one** shop; the other 39 continue with the old system. The pilot shop changes over (often directly, sometimes in parallel), and for some weeks its staff and customers use the new system for real. Problems are recorded and fixed; the user guide and the training are improved. When the pilot is successful, the system is **rolled out** to the other shops — either all at once or in groups — and the pilot staff, who now know the system well, help to train their colleagues.

The pilot limits the risk to **one site**, gives a realistic test with real workload, and produces experienced users who can support the rest of the organisation. It works best when the organisation has **several similar units** (shops, branches, schools, classes), so that what works in one will work in the others. Its limitations are that the full rollout is slower, that for a time two different systems are in use (data from the pilot shop may have to be combined with data from the others), and that the pilot site may not be typical — a small shop in a quiet district may not reveal the problems of a busy one in the city centre.

blocks.title: Pilot implementation
rows: If the system fails, **only one part** of the organisation is affected
Takes **longer** than direct changeover before everyone uses the system
Errors are found and fixed **before** the full rollout
The pilot site may not be **typical** of the others, so some problems appear later
Staff at the pilot site can **train** other staff later
Two different systems are in use in the organisation at the same time
Cheaper and less risky than running parallel everywhere
If the pilot fails, that department is still badly affected

blocks.title: When pilot implementation is suitable
blocks.content:
- A **supermarket chain** tries a new checkout system in **one shop**.
- A **school** introduces a new club-management system for **one grade** before the whole school.
- A bank tests new software in **one branch** of its network.

Phased implementation divides the **system**, not the organisation. A school's new information system may have modules for attendance, marks, timetables and reports to parents. In phase 1 **everyone** in the school starts using the attendance module, while marks, timetables and reports are still done the old way. Only when attendance works well does phase 2 — marks — begin, and so on. Each phase is a small changeover of its own, and each can be done directly or with a short period of parallel running.

Because each step is small, problems affect only **one function** and are easier to locate and fix; staff learn the system **gradually**; and the cost of hardware, training and support is **spread over a longer period**. The main difficulty is that, during the changeover, **old and new parts must work together**: the new marks module may need pupil lists from the old system, or the old report program may need marks from the new database. Building these temporary links is extra work and a source of errors. Phased implementation is also the **slowest** way to get the full benefit of the new system, and it is only possible when the system really can be split into **fairly independent modules**.

Methods can also be **combined**: a bank may run a pilot in one branch and, inside that branch, use parallel running for the first month; a hospital may introduce its modules in phases and pilot each phase in one department first.

blocks.title: Phased implementation
rows: If one module fails, only **that part** of the system is affected
**Slowest** method — the full system is in use only after all phases
Staff learn the system **gradually**, one part at a time
Old and new parts must **work together** (interfaces), which can be complex
Errors in each phase are fixed before the next
Requires careful **planning** of the order of phases
The benefits of the complete system arrive late

blocks.title: When phased implementation is suitable
blocks.content:
- A large **ERP** system: first **accounts**, then **stock control**, then **payroll**.
- A school system: first **attendance**, then **marks**, then **reports to parents**.
- Any system that can be divided into **independent modules**.

blocks.title: Pilot and phased — the pair students confuse

blocks.content:
- Describing pilot as "a small part of the system is introduced first" — that is **phased**. Pilot = **whole** system, **one place**.
- Saying pilot "has no risk" — the pilot site itself is still affected if the system fails.

blocks.title: The four methods compared
rows: Risk if the new system fails
Old system at the other sites
Small, simple or non-critical systems; old system unusable

blocks.caption: Choosing an implementation method — questions to ask about the scenario

blocks.text: The factors that decide the choice

blocks.content: No method is best in every situation; each is a **trade-off** between speed, cost and risk. When choosing, analysts look at the following factors of the scenario.

**How critical the system is.** Ask what happens if the new system stops working for a day. For a café's online menu, staff take orders by hand — an inconvenience. For a hospital's prescription system or a port's ship-tracking system, errors could harm people or cause large financial losses. The more critical the system, the more the organisation should pay for safety — parallel running, or at least a pilot.

**The structure of the organisation.** An organisation with **many similar sites** (a chain of shops, a network of schools, bank branches) is a natural candidate for a pilot. A single site with a system made of **separate modules** suits phased implementation. A small organisation with one simple system usually has no real choice except direct changeover.

**Budget and staff.** Parallel running needs money for overtime and staff who are able to do double work for weeks. If the organisation cannot afford this, a safer-than-direct alternative is a pilot or phased approach.
**Time.** If the new system is needed by a fixed date (a new law comes into force, the old software licence expires), the slower methods may not be possible.

**How similar the old and new systems are.** Parallel running requires that both systems can process the same data and produce comparable results. If the new system works in a completely different way (for example online self-service instead of paper forms handled by staff), parallel running may make no sense.
**How well the new system has been tested.** A system that has been used successfully by other organisations is less risky than custom software used for the first time.

In an exam answer, the method you choose matters less than the **justification**: a reason taken from the scenario and, for an evaluation, an honest disadvantage of the chosen method for that organisation.

blocks.title: How to choose and justify a method for a scenario
items: How **critical** is the system? If failure is dangerous or very costly → **parallel**.
Does the organisation have **several similar sites** (shops, branches, classes)? → **pilot**.
Can the system be split into **independent parts**? → **phased**.
Is it **small**, cheap, urgent, or is the old system **unusable**? → **direct**.
**Justify** with details from the scenario, and mention the **trade-off** (cost, time, risk).

blocks.title: Choose the method — four scenarios
blocks.content:
| Situation | Method | Reason linked to the scenario |
|---|---|---|
| A system that tracks the arrival of cargo ships at the Aktau seaport is being replaced | **Parallel** | Critical; errors could cause accidents or losses, so the old system is kept as a backup and results are compared |
| A school introduces a new system for managing hobby clubs, first for one grade | **Pilot** | Tried on one grade before all students use it; problems affect only that grade |
| A café lets customers order electronically instead of ordering from staff | **Direct** | Small, simple and not critical; quick and cheap; staff can take orders by hand if it fails |
| A city hospital replaces patient records, prescriptions and billing over a year | **Phased** | Large system with separate modules introduced one at a time; staff learn gradually |

blocks.title: Worked evaluation — a national bank's payment system [6-mark style]
blocks.content:
**Scenario:** a national bank is replacing the software that processes all customer payments.
- **Direct:** fastest and cheapest, **but** if the new software fails, no payments can be made anywhere — unacceptable for a bank.
- **Pilot:** one branch first limits the risk, **but** payments move between all branches, so a single branch cannot easily use a different system.
- **Phased:** modules (card payments, transfers, loans) one at a time, **but** old and new modules must exchange data, which is complex for money.
- **Parallel:** both systems process every payment and the results are compared; the old system is a backup. **Most expensive** and double work, **but** the bank can afford it and errors would cost far more.
- **Recommendation:** **parallel running**, because the system is critical and every result can be checked before the old system is switched off.

For "choose and justify" questions: **name** the method (1), give a reason **linked to the scenario** (1), and — if asked — a disadvantage **for that organisation** (1). "Parallel because it is safe" is weaker than "parallel because a fault in ship-tracking could cause accidents, and the old system stays as a backup".

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: List the four methods of system implementation. [2]**
Direct, parallel, pilot, phased (any two for 1 mark, all four for 2).

**Q: Describe parallel running. [2]**
The old and new systems run at the same time / the same data is entered into both (1); results are compared and the old system is stopped once the new one is shown to work (1).

**Q: Choose one type of system implementation that could be used by a clinic replacing paper patient records, and give one advantage and one disadvantage. [3]**
Parallel (1). Advantage: the old records remain as a backup / results can be compared (1). Disadvantage: expensive / double work for the staff (1).
*(Or direct: advantage — fastest / cheapest; disadvantage — very risky, no backup.)*

**Q: Compare pilot and phased implementation. [2]**
Pilot introduces the whole system in one part of the organisation first (1), whereas phased introduces the system one module at a time across the whole organisation (1).

**Q: Explain one disadvantage of direct changeover for a supermarket's checkout system. [2]**
If the new checkout software fails there is no old system to fall back on (1), so the shop cannot sell goods / loses sales and data until it is fixed (1).

**Q: Explain why parallel running is the most expensive method. [2]**
Two systems must be run and maintained at the same time (1), and staff enter the same data twice / need extra time or overtime (1).

- Confusing **pilot** (one **location** gets the **whole** system) with **phased** (everyone gets **one part** at a time).
- Saying parallel running is "fast" — it is the **slowest and most expensive**, but the **safest**.
- Choosing a method without **linking** the reason to the scenario.
- "Compare" answers that describe only **one** method — use **whereas** and say something about **both**.

blocks.title: Check yourself
items: List the four implementation methods and describe each in one sentence.
Give two advantages and two disadvantages of each method.
Which method is the safest? The fastest? The cheapest? The slowest?
Explain the difference between pilot and phased implementation with an example of each.

Choose and justify a method for: a new airline booking system; a new library system for a network of 20 schools; a new online menu for a small café; a new school system with attendance, marks and reports modules.
